editions.title: Nvidia shares slide as reports of Jensen Huang's ouster mount
editions.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports say its board may move against CEO Jensen Huang. Here's what we know.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is Nvidia. Its shares fell more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday and slid a further 7 to 8 per cent in after-hours trading on Wednesday, after the Wall Street Journal and New York Times reported that the board could meet as soon as the same day to decide the future of chief executive Jensen Huang. The reports follow Huang's admission of an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence agent, and a further alleged affair with Nvidia's vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell. Nvidia has hired former US attorney Joon H. Kim's firm to investigate, and US lawmakers have asked Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Nvidia has not responded to comment requests, and the ouster reports remain unconfirmed rumours. Related chip stocks, including Korean memory makers and TSMC, are being watched for knock-on effects.

Elsewhere, the AI and chip economy kept generating deals. TSMC's board has reportedly approved up to $1 billion of investment in OpenAI and Anthropic, which would give the chipmaker direct stakes in two of its biggest customers, though analysts have flagged circular financing concerns. London chip designer Fractile raised $720 million at a $7 billion valuation, and South Korea's president said Samsung's packaging expansion could spur about $30 billion of further investment. Google DeepMind also unveiled AlphaProof Code, which formally verified the cryptographic core of Signal in four weeks.

On the consumer side, Google Wallet added digital home keys, Google Fi previewed a dual-carrier "super network", and reports suggest Grand Theft Auto VI has passed $1 billion in sales ahead of its 19 November release, a figure not yet confirmed by Take-Two. Regulators also acted: New York forced T-Mobile to drop data caps on low-income home internet plans, and Germany reportedly banned Chinese drones from military bases.

editions.title: Anthropic IPO talk builds as Nvidia's Huang faces FBI probe
editions.notification: Anthropic's IPO valuation talk climbs towards $1.5tn while Nvidia shares slide over the Huang probe.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is the twin pressure on Nvidia and the surge of talk around Anthropic. Nvidia shares fell 4.3% on Monday, wiping roughly $190bn off its market value, after a class action accused the company and chief executive Jensen Huang of misleading shareholders over his alleged affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive whom US authorities reportedly concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia says it is running an independent investigation, and Donald Trump said the FBI was looking into the matter. Related reports tie Alice Huang to more than $7bn of Nvidia chip sales to China, which could strengthen bipartisan calls to tighten chip export controls.

Anthropic dominated the AI news. The Financial Times reports the company is considering an IPO at up to $1.4tn, with bankers reportedly preparing to lift the target to $1.5tn or more, and Goldman Sachs projects revenue above $600bn by 2030. These are rumours and forecasts, not confirmed plans. The company also released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with company-reported gains in coding and research and lower prices, and expanded Claude into a workspace with spreadsheets, whiteboards and data tools.

Elsewhere, AMD detailed its Zen 6 core and its Venice-X and Verano server chips, Alibaba's T-Head filed for a Hong Kong IPO, and the FCC is weighing a ban on Chinese optical transceivers that Microsoft is lobbying against. Regulation was also in focus, with a Paris Call on AI safety signed by ten AI companies but no deadlines or sanctions, and Australia recommending a new AI regulator after an OpenAI-linked breach.

editions.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang faces board probe over spy reports
editions.notification: Nvidia's CEO is under an independent probe over reported China spy links. Here's what we know so far.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the crisis at Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has apologised in an internal memo for an affair, after The New York Times reported that US agencies were examining Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, over suspected links to China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, supported by outside counsel, and says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang remains CEO. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November, and Singapore has opened its own probe into Megaspeed. The Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage allegations, and no one has been charged. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

The episode matters well beyond gossip. Nvidia sits at the centre of AI chip supply, and Megaspeed reportedly bought billions of dollars of its chips, while the US Commerce Department has accused the firm of smuggling $2 billion of advanced chips to China. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in a single session, their steepest daily drop since January 2025, amid a wider chip sell-off that also hit Asian markets. Analysts such as Jeffrey Sonnenfeld put Huang's chances of surviving the probe at roughly even.

Elsewhere, the AI-infrastructure backlash is gathering pace. A new analysis found about 90% of public comments at local government meetings opposed data centres, a Michigan Democrat who campaigned against them won a seat in Congress, and a Texas town-level ban passed with about 77% support. Samsung and SK hynix together hold 329 trillion won in cash, funding record chip spending and shareholder returns.

editions.notification: Tech shares slump after the midterms, Tesla winds down Cybertruck, and Anthropic eyes a pre-Thanksgiving IPO.
editions.intro:
Tech markets were rattled this week. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4 percent on Thursday, partly recovering on Friday, as rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and Democratic midterm wins raised fears of slower data-centre construction. Tesla shares fell 11 percent after Elon Musk said Cybertruck production will wind down around mid-2027, with the Texas plant shifting to the Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus robots. SpaceX dropped 9 percent in the same session, and Musk's fortune reportedly fell by $113bn.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic is reportedly pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving, seeking $80 to $100 billion at a valuation of $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below some investors' hopes. OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its funding-round target and raised only about a third of what it sought, though a separate report claims $11bn new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. Both are unconfirmed in the material provided.

Nvidia faces its own storm. Three House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Jensen Huang over reports that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have been recruited by China's intelligence services. Nvidia says its customer contacts are routine, and China has dismissed the claims. Meanwhile, the memory boom continues: DRAM prices are soaring, Samsung's cash pile passed 200 trillion won, and Raspberry Pi and Oppo are feeling the squeeze. Samsung's Taylor, Texas plant may start trial runs in December.

top_stories.summary: The FT reports Anthropic wants to raise $80 to $100 billion before Thanksgiving at $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below the $2 trillion some hoped for. The move comes amid a broad tech sell-off, and OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its own funding target.

top_stories.summary: House chairs have asked Nvidia's chief to explain links to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly watched by US agencies over China ties. Neither has been charged, and Nvidia says it would be warned if the government saw a threat.

top_stories.title: Samsung's Texas foundry may begin trial runs in December
top_stories.summary: Samsung's Taylor plant could start trial operations in mid-to-late December, with mass production next year. The site is expected to make Tesla's AI6 chips under a $16.5 billion deal, though the project is about two years late.

top_stories.title: No end in sight for the GPU and memory squeeze
top_stories.summary: DRAM prices are reportedly up about 400 percent since 2024, and Nvidia's RTX 5090 sells well above its launch price. Major memory makers are shifting capacity to AI memory and expect tight supply through 2027 and 2028.

top_stories.title: Samsung's cash pile passes 200 trillion won
top_stories.summary: Samsung reported 214.8 trillion won in cash at the end of Q3 and plans record capital spending of 84.4 trillion won. It can return 90 to 110 trillion won to shareholders this year.

top_stories.summary: METR's audit suggests Anthropic's rate of model improvement has roughly doubled, with much of the speed-up attributed to AI helping its own research. METR still rates acute catastrophic risk as low, but says the public risk report understated the acceleration.

Finance.title: Nvidia slides as Huang scandal hits markets
Finance.notification: Nvidia shares fall more than 11% in two days as the Jensen Huang scandal deepens and lawsuits follow.
Finance.summary:
The biggest story is the scandal around Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares fell a further 6.7% on Tuesday and more than 11% since Monday, valuing the company at about $4tn and letting Microsoft overtake it as the second most valuable company. The fall followed reports of Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence reportedly regards as a Chinese asset, and a class action has been filed. Reports say the board is weighing his position, though Trump has said he stands by him.

The wider backdrop is hawkish. October US consumer prices rose 0.4%, above forecasts, and markets have priced in a December Federal Reserve rate rise. That pushed Treasury yields higher, lifted the dollar and weighed on Asian bonds and currencies, with Indonesia's rupiah at a record low. Oil eased on hopes of a US-Iran deal, with Brent near $91 a barrel, while the UK FTSE 100 closed lower.

Investor nerves about whether AI spending will pay off run through many of these stories, from CoreWeave's sentiment problem to Nscale's possible listing delay and Anthropic's large IPO.

World.title: Nvidia shake-up and US political strains dominate
World.notification: Nvidia's board reportedly weighs ousting Jensen Huang as shares slump and a spying probe widens.
World.summary:
The biggest story in the region is Nvidia. Reports say its board is preparing to remove founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, possibly as soon as Wednesday, after claims of extramarital affairs and an alleged link to a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares have reportedly fallen sharply, with a reported $600 billion sell-off this week, and the company has not commented on the board meeting. Congressional Republicans have also threatened a subpoena over the same matter. These are largely unconfirmed reports, but they put a major AI chip supplier under pressure at a time when investors are already watching the chip sector closely.

Elsewhere in Washington, the political backdrop is turbulent. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment push when the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles to committee, although Democrats could revive the effort next year. A hotter-than-expected October inflation report has raised the prospect of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December, lifting the dollar to a 19-month high and weighing on US stock futures.

The UK's main story is the arrest of a senior US Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, while a Labour poll lead adds to the political picture. Across Europe and Asia, the Abu Dhabi Ukraine talks, the EU budget standoff and Spain's general strike dominate, alongside Indonesia's vice-presidential resignation.

Tech.title: Nvidia shares slump as Jensen Huang's future is questioned
Tech.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports question whether chief executive Jensen Huang will keep his job
Tech.summary:
The dominant tech story today is the turmoil at Nvidia, the leading AI chip maker. Its shares fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading in the US on Wednesday, erasing a small regular-session rebound and extending losses of more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday. The drop followed media reports of a board meeting and further alleged affairs involving chief executive Jensen Huang, with a Wall Street Journal report saying the board could move as early as Wednesday. Reports also link one of the women involved to suspicions of Chinese intelligence activity, and US lawmakers want Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Several of these claims are unconfirmed rumours.

The episode is spilling into politics and supply chains. Washington is asking about exposure of sensitive information and Nvidia's dealings in China, and analysts say it could add momentum to bipartisan efforts to tighten controls on advanced chip flows to China. Korean chipmakers are assessing whether leadership uncertainty could affect their ties with Nvidia.

The wider AI sector is also in focus. Anthropic's planned IPO is reportedly being pitched at $1.5tn or more, with Amazon and Google, its largest investors, potentially set to gain heavily, while TSMC plans to take stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI. Taken together, the stories show how closely the fortunes of chipmakers, AI labs and their investors are now tied together.

Fashion.title: Capri names Boxford CEO as luxury leadership shifts
Fashion.notification: Capri reportedly picks an Estée Lauder veteran to succeed John Idol at Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story for luxury and fashion today is leadership change at Capri Holdings, the owner of Michael Kors, Versace and Jimmy Choo. Justin Boxford, a former Estée Lauder luxury beauty executive, is reported to be taking over from John Idol, who has led the group since 2003. The move follows reports that would-be buyers have been circling Capri since the failed Tapestry deal, so the appointment will be read as a step in the group's next phase.

Elsewhere, the sector is wrestling with the wider pressures on its customers. Gulf shoppers are reportedly cutting back on luxuries as war-linked inflation bites, and luxury groups are looking to the United States as their Chinese growth engine stalls. US inflation data for October also showed fashion prices staying elevated, with consumers trading down to discount brands. Meanwhile, Coach and Ralph Lauren are reported to be outperforming a weak China market.

Creative and brand news is mixed. Balenciaga has launched a Damien Hirst collaboration, Tod's creative director Matteo Tamburini has stepped down, and Zimmermann is setting out expansion plans including a Paris flagship. Separately, Rhode says it is on pace to become the fastest beauty brand to reach $1 billion in sales, while Coty is restructuring in France.

Tech.title: Nvidia chief Huang faces affair probe as AI shares wobble
Tech.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang admits an affair with an executive US officials reportedly linked to China. Shares slid.
Tech.summary:
The dominant tech story is the fallout around Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. He has acknowledged in an internal memo an affair with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based data centre company, after reports that US officials believed she had shared information with Beijing. Nvidia says no sensitive information was shared, its board has opened an independent investigation, and House Republican chairs want a briefing by 11 November. Nvidia shares fell more than 4% on Monday, and a class action has been filed in California.

The affair story sits against a wider sell-off in AI-related shares, which has pushed several Asian markets into bear territory, with Asian indices now rebounding. The same week brought a wave of AI and chip news: Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, reports suggest it is preparing an IPO at up to $1.4 trillion, and AMD said it expects to outsell Intel for the first time. Policy pressure is also rising, with Washington weighing tighter controls on advanced chip flows to China and the FCC considering a ban on Chinese optical transceivers.

Beyond chips, the UK is weighing whether its under-16 social media ban should reach marketplaces such as Vinted and eBay, and Apple faces scrutiny over subscription sign-ups in its US stores.

World.title: US midterm fallout, Iran de-escalation and hot inflation weigh on markets
World.notification: Hot inflation data, Trump's Iran signals and a Democratic House reshape the week's markets
World.summary:
The biggest story in world affairs today is the fallout from the US midterm elections, where Democrats have won the House and are expected to take the Senate. Trump has blamed the result on a 'giant step back' and a one-day stock loss of about $3 trillion, while Republicans are split over the Iran war and the push by Congressman Thomas Massie to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. Markets are also reacting to an October inflation report that came in hotter than expected and has raised talk of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December.

Trump says Iran is militarily 'effectively over' and that renewed strikes are unlikely, a message that helped push oil lower. Iranian officials remain doubtful, and European ministers at the G7 in Paris say they cannot rule out fresh escalation over the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi hosts the first trilateral Russia-Ukraine-US talks since February, with European leaders pressing to be included.

For investors, the picture is mixed: softer oil on diplomacy, a possible rate rise from inflation, and a new Congress that could bring tougher oversight of large companies, including Nvidia and tech firms.

Europe and Asia are seeing a split: Asian chip stocks rallied on strong AI demand and China's record trade surplus, while Seoul's Kospi endured a steep sell-off and emergency margin-loan relief.

Fashion.notification: New creative directors are reshaping luxury demand, and resale prices are following them
Fashion.summary:
The clearest thread in luxury today is the power of new creative directors. An eBay Watchlist report, published 10 November, shows searches for Matthieu Blazy rose 291% after his first Chanel collection, with Demna up 42% after his first Gucci show and Jonathan Anderson up 92% after his Dior debut. Resale is turning that attention into prices, with celebrity sightings also driving sales.

Creative change is reshaping the houses themselves. Martine Rose has been named creative director of Balenciaga, succeeding Pierpaolo Piccioli, a historic first for the house. Balenciaga is also marking the 25th anniversary of the Le City bag with a Damien Hirst capsule. Elsewhere, Vaccarello's final Saint Laurent show featured 49 gold looks, and Moncler's Remo Ruffini credits collaborations for keeping the brand relevant.

On the business side, On reported sales up 17.2% with Asia-Pacific growing 31.9%, while Safilo's nine-month adjusted EBITDA rose 32.7%. Brands are leaning on collaborations and new markets to keep momentum, even as The Children's Place, which owns Gymboree, has filed for Chapter 11 and is seeking a sale.

Tech.title: Nvidia shares slump as Jensen Huang's future is questioned
Tech.notification: Nvidia shares tumble as reports question whether chief executive Jensen Huang will keep his job
Tech.summary:
The dominant tech story today is the turmoil at Nvidia, the leading AI chip maker. Its shares fell more than 8 per cent in after-hours trading in the US on Wednesday, erasing a small regular-session rebound and extending losses of more than 9.5 per cent over Monday and Tuesday. The drop followed media reports of a board meeting and further alleged affairs involving chief executive Jensen Huang, with a Wall Street Journal report saying the board could move as early as Wednesday. Reports also link one of the women involved to suspicions of Chinese intelligence activity, and US lawmakers want Huang to attend a closed-door briefing. Several of these claims are unconfirmed rumours.

The episode is spilling into politics and supply chains. Washington is asking about exposure of sensitive information and Nvidia's dealings in China, and analysts say it could add momentum to bipartisan efforts to tighten controls on advanced chip flows to China. Korean chipmakers are assessing whether leadership uncertainty could affect their ties with Nvidia.

The wider AI sector is also in focus. Anthropic's planned IPO is reportedly being pitched at $1.5tn or more, with Amazon and Google, its largest investors, potentially set to gain heavily, while TSMC plans to take stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI. Taken together, the stories show how closely the fortunes of chipmakers, AI labs and their investors are now tied together.

Finance.title: Nvidia slides as Huang scandal hits markets
Finance.notification: Nvidia shares fall more than 11% in two days as the Jensen Huang scandal deepens and lawsuits follow.
Finance.summary:
The biggest story is the scandal around Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Nvidia shares fell a further 6.7% on Tuesday and more than 11% since Monday, valuing the company at about $4tn and letting Microsoft overtake it as the second most valuable company. The fall followed reports of Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, whom US intelligence reportedly regards as a Chinese asset, and a class action has been filed. Reports say the board is weighing his position, though Trump has said he stands by him.

The wider backdrop is hawkish. October US consumer prices rose 0.4%, above forecasts, and markets have priced in a December Federal Reserve rate rise. That pushed Treasury yields higher, lifted the dollar and weighed on Asian bonds and currencies, with Indonesia's rupiah at a record low. Oil eased on hopes of a US-Iran deal, with Brent near $91 a barrel, while the UK FTSE 100 closed lower.

Investor nerves about whether AI spending will pay off run through many of these stories, from CoreWeave's sentiment problem to Nscale's possible listing delay and Anthropic's large IPO.

World.title: Nvidia shake-up and US political strains dominate
World.notification: Nvidia's board reportedly weighs ousting Jensen Huang as shares slump and a spying probe widens.
World.summary:
The biggest story in the region is Nvidia. Reports say its board is preparing to remove founder and chief executive Jensen Huang, possibly as soon as Wednesday, after claims of extramarital affairs and an alleged link to a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares have reportedly fallen sharply, with a reported $600 billion sell-off this week, and the company has not commented on the board meeting. Congressional Republicans have also threatened a subpoena over the same matter. These are largely unconfirmed reports, but they put a major AI chip supplier under pressure at a time when investors are already watching the chip sector closely.

Elsewhere in Washington, the political backdrop is turbulent. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth survived an impeachment push when the House voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles to committee, although Democrats could revive the effort next year. A hotter-than-expected October inflation report has raised the prospect of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December, lifting the dollar to a 19-month high and weighing on US stock futures.

The UK's main story is the arrest of a senior US Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, while a Labour poll lead adds to the political picture. Across Europe and Asia, the Abu Dhabi Ukraine talks, the EU budget standoff and Spain's general strike dominate, alongside Indonesia's vice-presidential resignation.

Fashion.title: Capri names Boxford CEO as luxury leadership shifts
Fashion.notification: Capri reportedly picks an Estée Lauder veteran to succeed John Idol at Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story for luxury and fashion today is leadership change at Capri Holdings, the owner of Michael Kors, Versace and Jimmy Choo. Justin Boxford, a former Estée Lauder luxury beauty executive, is reported to be taking over from John Idol, who has led the group since 2003. The move follows reports that would-be buyers have been circling Capri since the failed Tapestry deal, so the appointment will be read as a step in the group's next phase.

Elsewhere, the sector is wrestling with the wider pressures on its customers. Gulf shoppers are reportedly cutting back on luxuries as war-linked inflation bites, and luxury groups are looking to the United States as their Chinese growth engine stalls. US inflation data for October also showed fashion prices staying elevated, with consumers trading down to discount brands. Meanwhile, Coach and Ralph Lauren are reported to be outperforming a weak China market.

Creative and brand news is mixed. Balenciaga has launched a Damien Hirst collaboration, Tod's creative director Matteo Tamburini has stepped down, and Zimmermann is setting out expansion plans including a Paris flagship. Separately, Rhode says it is on pace to become the fastest beauty brand to reach $1 billion in sales, while Coty is restructuring in France.
